newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Vultures seek rich pickings in toxic waste, orphans.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Vultures seek rich pickings in toxic waste, orphans.

text.p: Emerging country economies bursting with growth and low world interest rates are making life tough for investors with a strong taste for risk and fat profits.
Countries which once brought a glow of excitement to the speculator have been so successful in transforming their economies that many no longer need to offer huge returns to entice investors.

And so the vulture funds and other yield-hungry investors are being forced to try to snap up defaulted debt on the secondary market in countries that not long ago would have frightened off all but the most determined gambler.

"It's just this long, long hunt for value and yield. Probably one of the scary things is that most of this looks like it is being driven by far too much money. It's a yield hunt rather than any cold perceptions of credit (quality)," said Quintin Archard, who heads the Emerging Market Bond and Asset Trading Co Ltd.
"People are just going to have to accept lower yields," he said.

Toxic waste is the market term for the sovereign debt of such countries as Sudan or Liberia, which are considered so unlikely to repay their foreign creditors that old loans can be picked up for just a few cents for every dollar of face value.
Some prefer orphans -- the label for debt, such as Eurobonds, that has been issued by companies in the emerging world which have since gone bankrupt.
And if it all goes wrong, said one trader, then the old bonds can be put into frames to decorate executive offices or perhaps turned into quite attractive wallpaper.
EMERGING SOVEREIGN DEBT OUTSHONE OTHER MARKETS
Last year, the emerging sovereign debt market -- much of it restructered into Brady and other actively traded bonds -- outshone just about every other market in the world.
Buyers of old Soviet debt at the start of 1996 would have tripled their investment by the end of the year. The picture was much the same for former Yugoslav debt following the end of the Bosnian war.
Debt of the major Latin American countries, which triggered the Third World debt crisis in the 1980s, jumped 30 percent last year.
That boom has meant there just isn't much more room to go higher, so the hunt for huge capital gains encourages a taste for the increasingly exotic.

"There is a very tangible interest in these countries from the vulture funds, the very high yield funds. They are the old players looking for something new to play with," said Indosuez Capital analyst Bradley Wickens.
The money has already been coming in.

Even the debt price of Sudan, which is threatened with the ultimate in financial pariah status by possible expulsion from the International Monetary Fund, has risen 300 percent -- to six cents in the dollar.

The market is full of even brighter success stories, especially countries facing sanctions -- notably North Korea and Cuba -- where investors are banking on the economies coming back into the international fold and their debt being paid off.
Congo, Cameroun and Angola are others with the potential to make investors wealthy, assuming their debt is rescheduled or bought back, traders said.

The biggest headache is that unlike the billions of dollars in Latin American and East European debt, these countries have only relatively small amounts to offer and some of the wealthy indviduals who like to play the market prefer to deal in large sums.
"There's a lot of money coming in. But most of these markets have a very limited debt stock," said Peter Bartlett, senior trader at BNP.

However, Barlett and others said there are still opportunities out there in the market for sovereign debt, especially in the little known countries, where research is poor and high risks offer the chance of high returns.
As one emerging debt company said in its last Chistmas card to clients:
"The road to riches comes with risks -- illiquidity, bankruptcy, devaluation, war and assassination."
